The Alchemist. Ben Jonson's masterpiece of satirical comedy, set in plague-stricken London, where a con-artist alchemist, his female accomplice, and a smooth-talking servant systematically dupe a parade of victims with the promise of transmuting lead into gold or granting impossible desires.

Face, a servant, poses as a chemist's assistant. Subtle presents himself as a master of the hermetic arts. Doll Common plays the Queen of Faery and various other roles to trap their clients.

Their victims arrive in succession. Dapper, a lawyer, seeks gambling luck through a fairy's touch. Abel Drugger, a tobacco seller, craves alchemical prosperity. Sir Epicure Mammon, a merchant, obsesses over the riches and libertine delights that alchemy will procure. Mammon's monologues on his future pleasures are sublime in their excess, expressing unbridled appetite more eloquently than anything else in the play.

The con escalates as they promise transmutation, spirit communion, and personal transformation, extracting money, jewelry, and goods under various pretexts from each gullible mark. The scheme implodes when Surly, a cynical knight, penetrates the fraud and attempts exposure. Subtle and Doll escape before being fully apprehended, but Face ingratiates himself with his master Lovewit upon his unexpected return. Through quick thinking, Face survives by admitting to the scheme and throwing his partners under the wheel.

The final twist embodies the play's darker vision: Face keeps his place in the household, having profited and deflected blame. The con succeeds despite exposure because greed and gullibility are eternal, and Jonson presents this not as redemption but as the natural victory of wit over foolishness in Stuart London.
